Bibliographic coupling edges, weighted by the coupling strength

Source: R/coupling_strength.R
coupling_strength.Rd

Builds the edges of a bibliographic coupling network in which the shared references are not all equal: sharing a reference that few documents cite says more about the proximity of two documents than sharing a reference that the whole corpus cites. The weight is the coupling strength (Vladutz and Cook 1984; Shen et al. 2019) , a refinement of the coupling angle of coupling_angle() that gives each shared reference a weight decreasing with its number of citations, in the spirit of the inverse document frequency of information retrieval (Spärck Jones 1972; Salton and Buckley 1988) (see tf-idf).

Usage

coupling_strength(
  dt,
  source,
  ref,
  weight_threshold = 1,
  output_in_character = TRUE
)

Arguments

dt

A data frame or a data.table of direct citations, one row per link between a citing document and a cited reference. It is not modified.

source

Character scalar. The column of the citing documents: they are the nodes of the coupling network.

ref

Character scalar. The column of the cited references.

weight_threshold

Number. The minimum number of shared references for two documents to be linked (1 by default). It applies to the number of shared references, not to the weight.

output_in_character

Logical. If TRUE (default), the identifiers are also returned as character columns from and to, to build a tidygraph graph more easily.

Value

A data.table with one row per pair of documents sharing at least weight_threshold references: the identifiers in from and to (character if output_in_character = TRUE), the coupling strength in weight, and the original identifiers in Source and Target. Each pair appears once, with Source < Target.

Details

Write \(N\) for the number of citing documents in the table, \(f_j\) for the number of documents citing reference \(j\), \(R(A)\) for the references of document \(A\) and \(L(A) = |R(A)|\) for the length of its bibliography. The weight of the tie between \(A\) and \(B\) is

$$w_{AB} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R(A) \cap R(B)} \log(N / f_j)}{L(A) \, L(B)}$$

A reference cited by every document has weight \(\log(1) = 0\); a reference cited by two documents has weight \(\log(N/2)\). Contrary to the coupling angle, the denominator is the product (not the square root of the product) of the lengths, and the weight is not bounded by 1; the scale of the weights depends on \(N\), so that the weights are meaningful relative to each other within one call, not across calls. This is Eq. 7 of (Shen et al. 2019) , who use base-10 logarithms; the natural logarithm used here multiplies all the weights by the same constant (\(\ln 10\)), which changes no ranking and no correlation. Unlike coupling_similarity(), the lengths \(L\) are simple counts of references, not sums of idf weights.

Computing choices:

  • \(N\) is the number of distinct citing documents in the table, including those that share no reference with any other document;

  • \(L(A)\) counts all the references of \(A\), including those cited by no other document;

  • duplicated rows are counted once, a document citing itself is ignored, and rows with a missing identifier are dropped with a warning;

  • the table of the user is not modified;

  • if no reference is shared (or if no pair reaches weight_threshold), a zero-row table is returned, with a warning that says why.

Memory: like all the coupling functions, it first lists all the pairs of documents citing a same reference. A reference cited by \(n\) documents creates \(n (n - 1) / 2\) pairs, and very popular references can exhaust the memory. Since such references have the smallest weights, they can often be removed before the call with little effect on the result.

Why use it in research

In a corpus built around a topic (the stagflation literature, a journal, a decade of central-banking research), a few references are cited by most documents: they define the field but do not distinguish the documents within it. With the coupling angle, two documents sharing only such classics are as close as two documents sharing equally many rare references. The coupling strength corrects this, and makes the resulting network more suited to detecting sub-specialities. The cost is a measure that depends on the whole corpus: the weight of a tie changes if documents are added to the table, and is not comparable across corpora of different sizes (see below).

Intuition

Two economists who both cite the most famous paper of their field are not necessarily working on the same question; two who both cite an obscure working paper probably are. The coupling strength measures how surprising a shared reference is: a reference cited by a fraction \(f/N\) of the corpus has a surprise of \(\log(N/f)\), which is 0 for a reference cited by everybody and grows as the reference gets rarer. The tie is the total surprise of what two documents share, divided (as for the coupling angle) by the lengths of the two bibliographies. It is the same logic as the tf-idf of search engines, where a word found in every text does not help to find a particular one.

References

Salton G, Buckley C (1988). “Term-Weighting Approaches in Automatic Text Retrieval.” Information Processing & Management, 24(5), 513–523.

Shen S, Zhu D, Rousseau R, Su X, Wang D (2019). “A Refined Method for Computing Bibliographic Coupling Strengths.” Journal of Informetrics, 13(2), 605–615. https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1751157716300244.

Spärck Jones K (1972). “A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval.” Journal of Documentation, 28(1), 11–21.

Vladutz G, Cook J (1984). “Bibliographic Coupling and Subject Relatedness.” Proceedings of the American Society for Information Science, 21, 204–207.

See also

Other coupling measures: biblio_coupling(), coupling_angle(), coupling_descriptive(), coupling_jaccard(), coupling_similarity(), coupling_vladutz(), descriptive_terms()

Examples

library(biblionetwork)
coupling_strength(Ref_stagflation,
                  source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                  ref = "ItemID_Ref")
#>             from         to      weight     Source     Target
#>           <char>     <char>       <num>      <int>      <int>
#>    1:    1021902    1184127 0.005870237    1021902    1184127
#>    2:     214927    2207578 0.020008623     214927    2207578
#>    3:    1184127    2901822 0.006565523    1184127    2901822
#>    4:    1184130    2901822 0.009848284    1184130    2901822
#>    5:    1717556    2901822 0.002563412    1717556    2901822
#>   ---                                                        
#> 2712: 1111111122 1111111183 0.009224890 1111111122 1111111183
#> 2713: 1111111134 1111111183 0.005902349 1111111134 1111111183
#> 2714: 1111111146 1111111183 0.008853523 1111111146 1111111183
#> 2715: 1111111161 1111111183 0.002629546 1111111161 1111111183
#> 2716: 1111111182 1111111183 0.038292193 1111111182 1111111183

# A toy example: d1 and d2 share r1 and r2, each cited by 2 of the
# 4 documents, so w = 2 * log(4 / 2) / (3 * 2)
toy <- data.frame(doc = c("d1", "d1", "d1", "d2", "d2", "d3", "d3", "d4", "d4"),
                  ref = c("r1", "r2", "r3", "r1", "r2", "r3", "r4", "r4", "r5"))
coupling_strength(toy, source = "doc", ref = "ref")
#>      from     to    weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>     <num> <char> <char>
#> 1:     d1     d2 0.2310491     d1     d2
#> 2:     d1     d3 0.1155245     d1     d3
#> 3:     d3     d4 0.1732868     d3     d4
